**What you can say for certain (assuming the monitor's log is accurate and complete):**

- **Exactly one of the two exited:** East or West, not both and not neither.

**Caveats on "certain":**

- "Didn't log an exit" isn't proof the other worker is healthy. It could be hung, never started, or exited after logging stopped.

**How to find out which one:**

- **Liveness check:** see which worker is still running (process list, PIDs, health endpoint, heartbeats).
- **Per-worker logs:** each worker's own output may show a shutdown or crash at the matching timestamp.
- **Correlate timestamps:** match the aggregate exit time against each worker's last heartbeat, last log line, or supervisor/orchestrator events (systemd, k8s pod status, exit codes).
- **For next time:** include the worker ID in the exit event so the aggregate monitor records who exited, not just how many.

# How Our Static-Site Releases Work

A release has two steps, always in this order:

1. **Upload** every new asset (JS, CSS, images, fonts) under a **versioned name**, e.g. `app.3f9a1c.js` instead of `app.js`.
2. **Switch the manifest**, the small file (often `index.html` or a JSON map) that tells the browser which asset names to load, so it points at the new names.

We don't delete the previous release's assets afterward.

## Why versioned names?

Each file name refers to exactly one version of the file's contents. `app.3f9a1c.js` always means the same bytes. Because of that:

- CDNs and browsers can cache assets aggressively, often for a year, since the content behind a name never changes.
- Old and new versions can sit side by side on the server without conflicting.
- The manifest is the only thing that changes in a release, so it is the single place where "which version is live" is decided.

## Why the upload happens before the switch

The manifest switch is the moment the release goes live. Once a browser reads the new manifest, it immediately asks for the files that manifest names.

If we switched first and uploaded second, there would be a window where the manifest points at files that don't exist yet. Any user who loaded the page during that window would get 404s for scripts and stylesheets, which means a broken or unstyled page. With a large upload or a slow CDN propagation, that window could last a while.

Uploading first means every file the new manifest refers to is already in place when the switch happens. The release goes from "fully old" to "fully new" in one step, with no broken middle state.

**Rule of thumb:** never publish a pointer to something that isn't there yet.

## Why we keep the old assets

Switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already have the old one. Some examples:

- A user opened the site five minutes before the release. Their page is still running the old manifest, and it may lazy-load more chunks (a route, a modal, an image) that the old manifest names.
- A browser or CDN edge has the old `index.html` cached and keeps serving it for a little while.
- A tab has been open in the background for hours.

All of these clients will keep asking for the **old** asset names. If we deleted those files during the release, those users would hit 404s in the middle of a session, which typically shows up as a blank screen or a "chunk failed to load" error.

Keeping the old assets lets those clients finish their sessions normally. Next time they load the page, they get the new manifest and the new assets.

Old assets also make **rollback** easy. To revert, we point the manifest back at the previous names. Those files are still there, so there's nothing to re-upload.

## Summary

| Step | What could go wrong if skipped or reordered | How our process prevents it |
|---|---|---|
| Versioned names | Cache serves stale content under the same name | Each name maps to exactly one version |
| Upload before switch | New manifest references files that don't exist yet → 404s | All new files exist before anything points at them |
| Keep old assets | Users mid-session request old files → 404s | Old files remain for clients still on the old manifest; rollback is just a manifest switch |

The idea behind all three: **the manifest is the only thing that moves, and every name it could possibly point to, old or new, must exist when it does.**

Old assets do eventually get cleaned up, once they're older than any realistic session or cache lifetime. Check with the team for our exact retention window before pruning anything.

**Why the upload comes first.** The manifest is what tells a browser which asset files to request. If we switched it before the new files existed, any browser that loaded the new manifest in that window would request files that aren't there yet and get 404s, leaving pages broken or unstyled. Uploading first means every name the new manifest points to is already in place when the first browser reads it, so the switch is effectively atomic from a user's point of view.

**Why the old assets stay.** Browsers that fetched the previous manifest before the switch keep requesting the old asset names. This happens through lazy-loaded chunks, later navigation in a single-page app, or a long-open tab. Deleting the old files would break those sessions mid-use. Because each release uses distinct versioned names, old and new assets coexist without conflict, and older clients finish their sessions on a consistent set of files.

Versioned names also make caching safe. A given filename's content never changes, so browsers and CDNs can cache it indefinitely without serving a stale mix of old and new code.

**No, you can't say which worker exited from that log alone.** The record is symmetric: "one exit, no name" is equally consistent with East exiting or West exiting.

**What you can say for certain, assuming the monitor is accurate and complete:**

- **Exactly one of the two exited:** East or West, but not both and not neither.
- **The other one did not exit** during the monitored window.
- So "East exited" and "West exited" are mutually exclusive, and one of them is true. If you learn either worker's status, you know the other's.

**Caveat on "for certain":** All of this rests on the monitor's reliability. If it can miss events (sampling gaps, dropped log lines, a crash during restart), then "exactly one logged" only means "at least one exited," and both could have. A logged exit could also be spurious, such as a restart or misreported health check. Whether the exclusive-or holds depends on how much you trust the aggregate count.

**How to find out which one:**

- **Live state:** Check the process list, container or pod status, or the service manager (`systemctl status`, `docker ps`, `kubectl get pods`). The missing or restarted one is your answer.
- **Per-worker evidence:** Look for each worker's own logs ending abruptly, a changed PID or start time, an incremented restart count, or a heartbeat that stopped.
- **Correlated signals:** Look for an exit code or OOM-kill entry in the system logs (`dmesg`, `journalctl`) around the timestamp of the aggregate event, or a gap in either worker's metrics.
- **Going forward:** Have the monitor record the worker ID, PID, and exit code with each event so this ambiguity doesn't come up again.

# How our static-site release works

A release has two steps, and the order matters:

1. **Upload** every new asset (JS, CSS, images, fonts) under a *versioned* name, e.g. `app.3f9c2a.js` instead of `app.js`.
2. **Switch** the manifest (the `index.html` or manifest file that references assets) so it points at those new names.

We never overwrite or delete the previous release's assets as part of this.

## Why upload comes before the switch

The manifest is the only thing that decides what a browser loads. Once it changes, any browser that fetches it will immediately request the new filenames.

If we switched first, there would be a window where the manifest references `app.3f9c2a.js` but that file doesn't exist yet. Anyone loading the site then would get 404s and a broken page. On a CDN this window can be longer than you'd expect, because uploads take time to propagate.

Uploading first means every file the new manifest mentions is already in place when the manifest goes live. The switch then becomes a single, effectively atomic step: before it, everyone sees the complete old release; after it, everyone sees the complete new release. There's no half-deployed state.

It also makes failures safe. If an upload fails partway, nothing user-facing has changed. The orphaned new files are harmless, and you can retry.

## Why we keep the old assets

Switching the manifest doesn't affect browsers that already have the old one. For example:

- Someone opened the site five minutes before the release. Their page holds the old manifest, and it will lazy-load `settings.a1b2c3.js` when they click Settings.
- A cached HTML page (in a browser, CDN, or service worker) can still reference old names for a while after the release.

If we deleted the old assets at release time, those users would hit 404s mid-session: broken navigation, missing styles, chunk-load errors. Keeping the old files means every manifest that's still in circulation can resolve everything it references.

Old assets also make **rollback** trivial. Pointing the manifest back at the previous version works instantly because those files are still there. No re-upload is needed.

## Why versioned names make this work

Because each release's files have unique names, old and new can sit side by side with no conflicts. It also lets us cache assets aggressively (long `Cache-Control` / `immutable`): a given filename's contents never change, so a cached copy is never stale. Only the manifest needs a short cache lifetime.

## Rules of thumb

- Never overwrite an existing versioned file. New content means a new name.
- Never switch the manifest until the upload has fully finished and succeeded.
- Don't clean up old assets at release time. If we prune, it happens later, once those versions are well outside any realistic session or cache lifetime.
